title: Towards an Efficiently Simulated Quantum Approximate Optimisation
journal_or_venue: IEEE International Conference on Fuzzy Systems (FUZZ) 2025
abstract_summary: The paper outlines ongoing work to develop an energy-efficient, scalable simulator for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) using FPGA hardware. It describes a methodology leveraging state-vector simulation, precomputed diagonal cost operators, and a hierarchical FPGA architecture to accelerate mixer and cost operations, and reports initial design choices and planned benchmarking against CPU/GPU implementations.
methodology_description: The authors propose and design an FPGA-based simulator for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). They select a state-vector simulation strategy (rather than tensor networks) and discretise the continuous adiabatic evolution via Trotter-Suzuki to form the parameterised QAOA unitary. To accelerate the two QAOA primitives they (a) pre-compute the diagonal cost Hamiltonian (HC) as a cost vector to allow element-wise phase application (bitwise-XOR and popcount based) instead of gate-by-gate matrix multiplications, and (b) decompose the transverse-field mixer (UM) into pairwise single-qubit rotation updates (real/imag parts) and implement a hierarchical, multi-tier segmentation of the full 2^n state vector across FPGA regions. The architecture uses a read-compute-write streaming pipeline with local, pipelined pair-update modules (systolic/replicated pair-update units), DSP slices for constant multiplications by precomputed cos(β)/sin(β), CLBs for adds/subtracts and sign handling, BRAM for local buffering, and lookup-tables or CORDIC-like blocks for trigonometric precomputation. They target single-precision (complex-64) arithmetic as the baseline, explore fixed-point as an option, and plan a phased implementation: single-FPGA functional prototype (mixer + cost operators) then multi-FPGA scaling using a Hydra-AI cluster of Terasic TR5 Stratix V GX boards. The methodology also includes resource-aware floorplanning, optimised interconnects, and benchmark plans against existing CPU/GPU simulators/frameworks to evaluate execution time, scalability and power efficiency.
experimental_setup: Planned hardware target: Terasic TR5 Stratix V GX FPGA Development Kit (selected for HBM, high DSP slice density and on-chip memory). Development uses the university's Hydra-AI cluster of interconnected TR5 boards. Implementation targets single-precision floating-point complex arithmetic (complex-64). Architecture includes BRAM buffering, DSP slices for multiplications, CLBs for add/subtract and bitwise ops, pipelined systolic arrays for pair-update modules, and on-chip lookup/Tables or CORDIC-like blocks for trig functions. Initial stage: single-FPGA prototype; next stage: multi-FPGA networking and scaling.
key_findings: [supported] QAOA is a competitive variational quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimisation problems (COPs) that can be expressed as Binary Quadratic Forms (BQF).
[supported] QAOA can be seen as discretised (Trotterised) adiabatic evolution alternating between problem (HC) and mixer (HM) Hamiltonians parameterised by angles (β, γ).

[supported] Simulating QAOA on classical hardware (state-vector or tensor-network methods) is essential for verification, algorithm exploration, and performance profiling in the absence of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
[supported] State-vector simulation is straightforward and often preferred for deep QAOA circuits but is limited by exponential memory growth (size 2^n for n qubits).
[supported] Tensor-network methods can simulate larger circuits in some cases but become less effective for high-depth QAOA circuits.

[supported] Precomputation of the diagonal cost Hamiltonian (as used in QOkit and JuliaQAOA) speeds up application of the cost operator by avoiding explicit gate sequences and enables efficient element-wise updates.

[supported] The mixer (transverse-field) layer is the major computational bottleneck in QAOA state-vector simulation because single-qubit rotations couple amplitude pairs across the full state vector.

[supported] Current large-scale QAOA simulators commonly rely on GPU acceleration (cuQuantum, CUDA implementations) and have advanced state-vector performance but face limits in power, memory and bandwidth.

[supported] FPGAs offer architectural features beneficial to quantum simulation (custom pipelines, massive parallelism, DSP slices, low latency, and potentially lower power consumption) and prior works have explored FPGA-based quantum simulation.
[speculative] To the authors' knowledge there is no scalable FPGA-based QAOA simulator in the literature (claim of absence).

[speculative] An FPGA implementation that uses hierarchical multi-tier segmentation of the state vector, pipelined DSP-based complex arithmetic, BRAM streaming, and precomputed cost vectors can achieve scalable, energy-efficient QAOA state-vector simulation and may outperform CPU/GPU approaches on throughput and power-efficiency.

[speculative] Employing a Terasic TR5 Stratix V GX FPGA (and a Hydra-AI multi-board environment) with single-precision complex arithmetic is a feasible design choice for prototyping and scaling FPGA-based QAOA simulation.
[supported] Memory bandwidth, limited on-chip memory, and inter-FPGA / host communication overhead are key bottlenecks that must be addressed for scalable FPGA-based simulation.

[supported] Pre-computation (lookup tables, CORDIC-like blocks) of trig/exponential constants and optimising fixed vs floating point are practical optimisations to reduce FPGA resource usage and latency.

[supported] Integrating classical optimisers (including fuzzy and learning-based optimisers) that require fewer iterations can reduce costly FPGA–host communication and overall latency in hybrid quantum-classical workflows.

[speculative] Planned benchmarking against CPU/GPU simulators (Qiskit Aer, cuQuantum, JuliaQAOA, QOkit) will quantify execution time, scalability and power-efficiency benefits; these evaluations are future work.
results_summary: This conference paper reports a methodological and architectural study (no completed hardware results) for accelerating QAOA state-vector simulation using FPGAs. It reviews QAOA structure and existing CPU/GPU simulation approaches, identifies the mixer layer and memory bandwidth as primary bottlenecks, and proposes a hierarchical, pipelined FPGA architecture that leverages precomputed diagonal cost vectors, DSP slices for complex arithmetic, BRAM streaming, and multi-tier state-vector segmentation. The authors have selected a Terasic Stratix V GX board for prototyping within a multi-board Hydra-AI environment, discussed precision and resource trade-offs, and outlined planned benchmarks and real-world application tests. Empirical implementation and performance evaluations are stated as ongoing/future work.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper cites prior literature that QAOA has potential to outperform classical solvers on some COPs and argues that FPGA-accelerated simulation could enable larger-scale exploration, but provides no empirical demonstration of quantum advantage; claims about FPGA outperforming GPUs/CPUs are presented as planned/expected and remain speculative pending benchmarking.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — QAOA is framed as a competitive NISQ-era variational algorithm for combinatorial optimisation problems (BQF/QUBO) and thus a target for near-term study.
#idea:hybrid-approach — The proposed workflow integrates classical optimisers with FPGA-accelerated state-vector simulation to reduce FPGA–host communication and overall hybrid loop latency.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Authors assert QAOA's competitiveness for COPs and speculate that an energy-efficient FPGA simulator may enable faster exploration of QAOA parameter landscapes versus CPU/GPU baselines.
#limitation:qubit-count — State-vector simulation is limited by exponential memory (2^n) growth; memory bandwidth and on-chip memory are identified as primary bottlenecks for scaling.

#limitation:simulation-only — The paper presents an architectural and methodological design without completed hardware results or benchmarking; implementation and performance evaluation are future work.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Claims about throughput and power-efficiency gains of the FPGA approach are speculative and planned to be validated in future benchmarks against GPU/CPU simulators.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Practical FPGA optimisations proposed include precomputed diagonal cost vectors, pair-update systolic modules for mixer operations, BRAM streaming and DSP-based complex arithmetic to accelerate state-vector updates.
contradictions: The authors claim (speculatively) there is no scalable FPGA-based QAOA simulator in the literature, yet the paper also notes prior works exploring FPGA-based quantum simulation — an internal contradiction about the prior-art landscape and scalability claims.

The paper speculates that an FPGA implementation may outperform GPU/CPU approaches in throughput and power-efficiency, but provides no empirical benchmarks; this conflicts with the acknowledged state of the art where GPU-accelerated simulators (cuQuantum/CUDA) currently demonstrate leading state-vector performance.
